doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Blues, Louis Armstrong and keeping it alive
summary: He argues the blues should not be dismissed as degrading, praises Armstrong's dues, and says blues stays in his own playing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: Do you think that some of the younger generation got to the point where they felt the blues was denigrating to their culture?

That’s a good question. That’s a very good question. It could be, but you know my dad used to say to me there’s a reason for everything but there is no excuse for anything. So don’t make that your excuse not to learn the blues. Because the blues is something real. And it’s got a real place in jazz. So I mean you can hey man it’s degrading or it’s Uncle Tom or whatever, I mean it’s just, don’t use the excuse, because of that that’s why I don’t play the blues. When you think of Louis Armstrong himself, the dues that that guy paid that no one had to pay after him. Every jazz musician is standing on Louis Armstrong’s

shoulders. Every one. I mean he didn’t have too many, I mean he had Joe Oliver as a mentor, he had a few guys, B.A. Rolfe that he heard play, but he pretty much single- handedly revolutionized jazz and just did the whole thing man. Everything after him was affected by him. He and like Michaelangelo are like two of the greatest artists. I mean the world just was not the same after these guys. And I mean this is before mass media. Oh man, Louis Armstrong, I mean to be a black man, and I’m not talking a Creole man that could get by in the brown side of town, this was a black guy man, with very little education, came from, his mother was in black Storyville — I didn’t know exactly how she made a living, she had a questionable way of making a living I say, and to become Louis Armstrong. That doesn’t happen every day. It’s never going to happen again as a matter of fact.

No. And so I mean the blues was good enough for Louis Armstrong man, and good enough for Charlie Parker, and good enough for Roy Eldridge and Coleman Hawkins, and Prez, and all of these cats, all the way through Miles, Clifford Brown, Diz, and then kind of all of a sudden it started to diminish when we could justify that we really wanted to get serious or whatever. And I think blues is serious man, it’s very serious. Because it’s something from within, not something acquired. It’s a statement from within.
Well I’m sure you’re going to keep it alive in your own playing.
Oh man, I like playing, attempting to play some more modern forms and stuff like that, but whenever I think of the way I like to play it’s a very, very strong blues element in there.
